PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF THE SHAHANSHAH AND EMPRESS OF IRAN
speechtext:
This House is honoured today by the presence in the Speaker's Gallery of His Imperial Majesty the Shahanshah of Iran and the Empress Farah Pahlavi.
Their Imperial Majesties are paying a most welcome one week visit to Canada as official guests of this country. The purpose of this royal visit is to strengthen the links between Canada, as a representative member of the western community of nations, and the State of Iran.
I am sure I speak for all hon. Members of this House in expressing to His Imperial Majesty our admiration for the courageous and unprecedented steps he has taken toward the social betterment of his own people, particularly in the highly important area of education and in the vital field of land reform.

Knowing that Their Majesties have also an admirable command of French, perhaps I might be allowed to say a few words in that language to convey our very special thanks to Her Imperial Majesty Farah Pahlavi, whose vernal charm is bringing us a living image of the Orient.

May I extend to Their Imperial Majesties the felicitations of this House and the sincere hope that they will take home with them nothing but pleasurable memories of this country and its people.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF THE SHAHANSHAH AND EMPRESS OF IRAN
speechtext: Hear, hear.

He has also had discussions with the British mission, with the French and Israeli ambassadors, in addition to other missions. Naturally he has had talks with the American ambassador and he has seen the Papal Nuncio, the dean of the diplomatic corps, who, as the House knows, has played a very active role in developments in Santo Domingo. He has had discussions with General Rikhye who is heading the United Nations observer group until such time as the representative of the Secretary General reaches the Dominican Republic.
Today's news of the situation in that country is conflicting, and I would prefer to have today's events assessed and analysed before I make any observations in the House. But I may say that both the Caamano regime and the Imbert regime have sought recognition from other countries, including Canada. The Prime Minister stated on May 11 that he did not consider Colonel Caamano had established a claim for recognition. We have since received a request for recognition from General Imbert. We feel that the situation there is such that neither regime warrants recognition by Canada until the situation takes on a much more stabilized character than at the present time.
In his report of yesterday our special representative stressed the need for a stricter observance of the cease fire which was earlier negotiated by the Organization of American States and which has been reiterated by the Secretary General of the United Nations, and indeed by the security council. The Organization of American States has asked the security council to take no action in the matter at the present time in the hope that, being on the ground, it might be able to assist in bringing about some accommodation and perhaps a cease fire, which thus far it has not succeeded in doing.

speechtext: It is a pressing question. I wanted to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration if it is correct that five United States citizens who were seeking admission to Canada at Douglas, B.C., for the purpose of taking part in a peace demonstration were denied admission to this country by his Department.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
maintopic: REPORTED DENIAL OF ENTRY OF FIVE U.S. CITIZENS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. Member asked this question because some communications on the subject have been received and I have had occasion to look into it. My reply might be somewhat lengthy, but I think the circumstances merit it.
On Monday afternoon, May 17, five United States citizens attempted to enter Canada at the port of Douglas. The usual inquiries were conducted by an officer of my department and the applicants stated that they wished to join a peace march that was being organized to protest against certain installations at Comox, B.C. All the individuals concerned were unemployed. Some of them seemed to
May 20. 1965	COMMONS
be without much in the way of funds. They were subjected to the usual questioning prescribed by the Immigration Act and they withdrew their applications and returned to the United States.
At four o'clock on the morning of Wednesday, May 19, the same five people appeared in an automobile at another border port, a few miles away, and when they were subjected to the same type of questioning they again withdrew.
At five o'clock in the afternoon on Wednesday, May 19, this group reappeared at the Douglas immigration office. This was their second visit to Douglas. They were asked by my departmental officials to come into the immigration office for questioning because it was raining. They refused to come in but stretched out on the tarmac in front of the building. After lying in the rain for some hours the applicants did come into the building. All five were interviewed. These facts came to light as a result of the investigations.
One member of the group is a 22 year old unemployed citizen of the United States. He was refused admission and ordered deported by the officers of my department. He was refused admission and ordered deported first because in 1958 he threw a seven year old girl from a rooftop and killed her. He was certified as insane and placed in a state hospital. Later he was released and charged with murder, convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He admitted that he was a parole violator, and naturally his admission was refused by my officers.
Another one in the same party, also 22 years old and who seemed to be the ringleader, had a police record in the United States dating back to July, 1963. He had been convicted and confined to a county jail for some time, for being a public nuisance. He had been certified as being mentally and morally unfit for military service in the United States. He gave his occupation as that of a professional marcher and stated that he had participated in marches in the United States, Russia and Mexico. He also was refused admission because of his record.
A third one had only $2 in his possession and he also admitted to a criminal record having been convicted and sentenced to from two to five years in Detroit, Michigan. He had served two years for carrying concealed weapons and he was also an admitted user of marijuana.
Some lion. Members: More, more.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1.	That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 36 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions "That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair"; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year. That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-two members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follow:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
May 20, 19G5	COMMONS
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.-

Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of appreciation for the attitude of the House yesterday during my absence on an appointment that was made weeks ago, and the adjournment which made it possible for me to follow the Prime Minister in this most important debate. I regret that I was absent while he made his speech yesterday, and today he did me the courtesy of informing me that he too would be absent when I replied. In his absence some references will not be made to some of the arguments that were advanced, because another opportunity to do so will occur when the debate takes place on the other portion of the proposals of the Government.
I say at once that I have read the Prime Minister's speech with great care. His summary of Parliament was succinct and complete, and in many ways I found it most interesting. However, naturally I do not agree with some of his contentions. I was greatly impressed by his reference to the rules in a hockey game as being comparable to the rules in Parliament.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, what we intend to guard against-using that analogy-is that there would not be much of a hockey game if one side were denied the carrying of hockey sticks. I am afraid that in some particulars
DEBATES	1511
House of Commons Procedures that will be the consequence of the action being taken by the Government in this connection.
I am making no formal speech today. I am going to deal in general with Parliament, with something of the meaning of this institution which so often through the ages has been criticized but still remains the embodiment of the great principles of freedom upon which it was founded.
Many outstanding contributions have been made by publicists to Parliament, but I know of no description of Parliament in more complete form than that by Right Hon. Quintin Hogg, M.P., who gave up his peerage to be in the House of Commons. In his book "The Purpose of Parliament" he said:
.. .Parliament is not like a building designed and constructed by a single architect, such as the Parthenon, St. Paul's Cathedral or the Empire State Building. Parliament resembles rather an ancient family mansion which has been lived in continuously for a period of centuries, and has served the needs of those that have dwelt therein by constantly modifying and adding to its conveniences from generation to generation.
When we speak of Parliament we think of this House as one of the major elements in Parliament. And when we think of the length of time that sessions take today, increasing each year, we begin to realize what the late Sir Winston Churchill meant when he said that if Parliament sits more than five or six months a year the life blood of Parliament is sapped away. I often hear people ask why we don't act in the Parliament of Canada the way they do in the British House of Commons. Those who say that know not the British House of Commons. Why are we so critical of one another? Why is there from time to time interruptions that sometimes deny a Member the opportunity to fully express himself?
Only a few days ago a leading university professor called on me. He advanced this argument and I said I was not particularly impressed with it. I told him I had with me yesterday's London Times and it showed that the day before-incidentally this is within the last month-the Minister of Defence in the United Kingdom had tried for 45 minutes to get the attention of the House and had not succeeded.
What would they say in the Parliament of Canada if someone were to use the expression Winston Churchill once used in his latter years, when he said, as he looked at the government-and I do not know what he would have said if he had looked at this
May 20, 1965

House of Commons Procedures Government-"Mr. Speaker, this is a lousy government," and immediately stated to the Speaker, "Now, before you call me to order, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it very clear that this description is not one of vituperative language but of anatomical exactitude."
I have seen the Parliament of Britain over and over again since 1916. Parliament lives in the crucible of strong discussion and effective argument. Parliament lives when you and I speak out for this institution rather than joining with those who, outside of Parliament, depreciate it, and have done so in every generation. One of the great authorities on parliament is Bernard Crick, and in a recent article in the London Observer, entitled "Poor Old Parliament" he wrote:
So frequently we hear it said that certain matters should be taken out of the realm of politics, national defence and social security and so on. What inspires such well meant nonsense is of course, downright distrust of Parliament, but a mistrust based on a misunderstanding.
Then he went on to say something that I think is particularly pertinent today in the light of the change in Parliament since the first world war, that the role of Parliament under modem conditions is best pictured as a permanent election campaign. This, he said, is not weakness as the prissies say, but it is real strength. It does not and could not govern but it controls governments indirectly through its effect on the electorate. Then he said that so often reforms are asked for that, if carried into effect, would place Parliament in the position of being emasculated.
Changes there must be, but the first consideration before all of us should be the preservation of the mission of Parliament. These sops in the form of periodical reforms, according to Bernard Crick, cannot but weaken the institution of Parliament.
I hear it said that Parliament has become ineffective, and people talk about the great old days. Well, I did not see Parliament before 1920 but I have seen it often since, and I heard the greatness of the parliamentarians during the Meighen regime, the latter part of the Borden regime, and so on through the years. There has been no change when you take the picture by and large.
I like to sit in this House and look at young Members coming in, and to listen to their arguments. They may not be particularly eulogistic of me, but I like to hear young men and women in the House showing that leadership and that infusion of new ability that comes from new and young Members in this Chamber.

They say Parliament is ineffective. That is not my view. Parliament is a place where ideas are tested, where in discussion the truth is found so far as humanly possible, and where the faulty is cast aside. End controversy in Parliament and you end Parliament.
Why is there this criticism? One reason is that people do not know what is going on in Parliament; but we down in this part of the Chamber, we who sit as Members, are not to blame. The responsibility is that of the agencies of public information to make available to the public reasonably full information on what is going on. It is so easy today to get wide publicity. If one were to arise in this House and cast some doubt on the paternity of an hon. Member opposite, that would be news; but so often-and I am not speaking of those who have been in Parliament a long time, I am speaking about the average private Member-so often the private Member burning the midnight oil produces a speech that is worthy of the people knowing of it, but there is not even a reference to the fact that the hon. gentleman or the hon. lady spoke.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
You cannot build Parliament that way. They say it is ineffective. I am going to mention something now that will not be as attractive to some Members as what I have just said. One of the most serious things about Parliament today is the absenteeism -and it has grown and grown with the years. You could get away, as a House, with absenteeism when we were getting $4,000, or $6,000 a year; but when we are getting $18,000, and $6,000 free of income tax, there is no justification for continued absence from this chamber.
What is going to happen unless this is remedied-by us, not by the Government? It must be remedied by each and every individual. We are going to place a Member of Parliament in the position of having what they have in the United States Congress, the roll call; and what they have in the Senate today. There will always be good reasons for absences; but Members Cannot justify not being here during the progress of votes when they should be voicing their decision. I make the appeal to reduce absenteeism, and apply it to no section of the House because it is something that applies in general. But I do point out that those who prate of Parliament and what should be done, should know that nothing-this is the way I find it; I
May 20, 1965

do not know how other hon. Members find it-is doing more harm to this institution than absenteeism.
Indeed, one of the interesting things as one reads history is to read the rules of Parliament in 1792 when Upper and Lower Canada joined together under the Constitutional Act. I had those rules, and they disappeared. Those rules of debate were much the same as the rules of debate today, with one exception. In effect the rule was that no Member should absent himself without cause, and when the Speaker noted his absence he should forthwith have him brought to the House by the sheriff.

I believe in reform, the need of bringing about changes to meet changing conditions. We did that when I was Prime Minister in the 1960-61 committees. I am not going to read what the present Prime Minister said, but he did say those committees had done good work. I recognize the need for change, provided that we weigh the results of these changes, not after the event but before the event. Parliamentary procedure represents the wisdom of generations. It is designed to achieve the objective of a full and purposeful discussion. But don't forget this fact, that it does not take long to move from the government to the opposition; and sometimes even less to move from the opposition to the government. We must remember, also, that in

I do not say that improvements are not necessary-because we led the way in that regard in the examination of expenditures. We decided that the practice of years, of having a Member of the party in power as chairman of the committee on expenditures, was not effective and we made the present Speaker chairman of that committee. We made various other changes regarding the length of time of debates. Where there are purposeful changes that can be made without enervating the House of Commons, those changes will be acceptable. What we must guard against are the dangerous short cuts.
I mention this today owing to the visit of United States Congressmen with us. In 1942 I had the honour to be the Chairman of the first conference which brought together members of the United States Congress and members of the various Parliaments of the Commonwealth. One of the matters we discussed at that time was Parliament and effective parliamentary institutions. Because of their presence today I should like to mention the very strong and effective words of a great Justice of the United States, Mr. Justice William O. Douglas, who said this:
History shows that Governments bent on a crusade, or officials filled with ambitions have usually been inclined to take short cuts. The cause being a noble one (for it always is), the people being filled with alarm (for they usually are), the Government being motivated by worthy aims (as it always professes), the demand for quick and easy justice mounts.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out what was said by the Prime Minister. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what is the reason for these changes? It is to help the private Members. This solicitude expressed by the Prime Minister is quite inconsonant with the kind of treatment hon. Members are receiving in the House when they ask questions. What I am going to say now is in the absence of that hon. gentleman who holds the position of the Speaker of the House.
The number one responsibility now before us is the establishment of a permanent Speaker. In 1957 I tried to bring before Parliament the name of an hon. gentleman in relation to this permanent Speaker position in order to bring about a completely nonpartisan Speakership. For reasons best known to him, and I refer to the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), he said that he thought the reason I did that was because I wanted to get him out of the House in order to deprive the House of his debating capacity. I had nothing like that in mind.

Our basic weakness is the lack of a permanent Speaker. I am going to say something now, in his ab-

I mentioned a moment ago the stand I took in 1957, and I still think what I thought at that time. I believe that you can alter the procedure of Parliament ad infinitum, but this House will not function as does the House in the United Kingdom, that Mother of Parliaments, until we have a permanent Speaker.
The present Prime Minister speaking in this House on September 27, 1962 said this about me:
The Prime Minister has mentioned the desirability, in certain circumstances in the future, of arranging for permanency in the office of Speaker.
I agree that if we could make arrangements in future which would provide for continuity in the holding of this very important office, having regard to our tradition that it should be held alternately by French speaking and English speaking Canadians, it might be a desirable thing to do. [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Why do we not do this now? We now have in that office a representative from a Montreal constituency. I should like to see Parliament attain all the greatness that each of us desires it to achieve. I do not believe in the principle that a constituency should be set up for the purpose of providing a Speaker. He would then cease to be the first Commoner that he is, because he would be there by choice and not election. The next Speaker will be of the French language and origin, but I speak now for my colleagues in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition when I say that in order to make the House effective we would, within our power, not contest the constituency of the present Speaker were he to be made permanent.
I do not want to say all of the things that are in my heart regarding the Speaker, but when I mentioned him a moment ago I was very pleased at the widespread applause in all parts of the House when I spoke of the attitude of the present Speaker. We will never be able to be nearer agreement as to two of the outstanding qualities of a Speaker, first, knowledge of Parliament, which carries with it the experience that can only come after years in the House and, second, that spirit of fairness and impartiality that has characterized the present Speaker. I read what Jennings has to say regarding the office of Speaker:

House of Commons Procedures
It is unnecessary to consider here the powers that he exercises by long standing practice... British experience shows that it is by no means impossible for a fair minded man deliberately to cast away his political bias and to attain a state of mind which is almost, if not quite, impartial. He is normally chosen, in the first instance, from among the Government majority. It is desirable that he should not have taken too prominent a part in party polemics.
The present Speaker has every one of these qualifications. Only twice in 70 years has a Speaker of the British House of Commons been opposed and, as Jennings says, the reason is that once he is appointed he divests himself of his party character and has no communications of a party character.
If we had a permanent Speaker our fears regarding certain portions of this package deal would be greatly lessened. But we have had the experience of 1956 which can never be eradicated from the hearts of those who passed through it. Sitting over there are some of those who belonged to that group in 1956 that caused the Speaker, with their connivance and support, to trample on Parliament and its rights and viciously disavow principles that had been accepted for 100 years. Let us have a permanent Speaker. There is unanimity now in the reaction to the present Speaker.
So far as the subject of questions is concerned, if the Government will give its undertaking that questions will be answered as they are in the United Kingdom, within three days, many of those questions that are asked today would become unnecessary. We could reduce the question period to half an hour.
I was glad to see that the Prime Minister had accepted three of the suggestions I had made for reform. There are a few others that I wish he had accepted when he was reading from what I had said. He referred with approval to what I said regarding supply motions. On March 9, 1964, as found on page 718 of Hansard, I said:
-I think that with six supply motions available in each session, with the exception of the first, which would last two days, the others might be restricted to one day. For after all, in the course of one day on a motion to go into supply there would be available to all parts of the House the opportunity to debate the amendment.
Then I went on to the subject of questions, and there has been no reform in that connection. Ministers have flouted Parliament with their insufficient and evasive answers. In the last year Parliament has been deceived by Ministers on three occasions that I know of. The Prime Minister's selective amnesia, as it was described by the hon. Member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume), caused
1518	COMMONS DEBATES	May 20. 1965
House of Commons Procedures him to say that he did not know until November what he had been told in September regarding the Rivard case. The Prime Minister quoted me with approval but I had hoped he would have gone a little further. I also said in 1964:
Next, we come to the question of the Government's responsibility in connection with questions. Some of the answers we have been receiving lately have been anything but complete, anything but informative, and their major quality has been the concealment of any information...
We have had the same thing in the last few days from the Minister of National Defence- evasion, concealment, information denied to the House to which it is entitled... I would point out, as the United Kingdom is referred to as an example of what should be done, that unstarred questions are answered in three days in the United Kingdom House.
I asked at that time that there should be no automatic adjournment at ten o'clock but that the House should continue when any Member was dissatisfied with the answer given to a question, and that recommendation was subsequently followed. In the period I have been in the House questions on orders of the day have expanded greatly. I reiterate that one of the major reasons for the lengthy question period is that this is the only way in which we can be assured of getting some kind of information.
I come now to the next point which the Prime Minister says has come to his mind because of his desire to increase the role of private Members. It is difficult for me to understand how the private Member is going to be strengthened by limiting his time. It is hard for me to understand how the private Member is going to be strengthened by curtailing the time for the discussion of estimates. I think the sending of estimates to committees is something worthy of support, not as a permanent fixture but to ascertain how it works out.
So far as the apportionment of time is concerned, unless the Speaker is a permanent Speaker it is a dangerous interference with Parliament. What the Government is proposing is that in the first hour they can say that this is going to be it. They can say they are going to give the Opposition a day to discuss a certain matter before they even find out what the stand of the Opposition is going to be. They are going to fix the time. Is it any wonder that the Globe and Mail had a cartoon depicting a guillotine with the Prime Minister talking to the President of the Privy Council and saying, "This is a particularly good idea, this will work well"?

[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The Prime Minister says the need for action in this regard is the expansion in legislation, particularly social welfare legislation. Social welfare, Mr. Speaker, was not born when this Government took office. This has been a continuing subject of legislation throughout the years. If there had been no debate, what would have happened to the original pension plan? When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) brought it in she gave us to understand that this was the greatest thing the mind of man, or even woman, had ever been able to devise. Then, the plan was put in drydock after criticism. What would have happened in the flag situation? They came in with the band playing and with three maple leaves on a single stem. We criticized and stood against it, so then they threw it overboard. If there had been this form of selective closure, what would have happened?
What about the $10 increase in old age pensions? What would have happened to it if they had this system whereby they can stifle criticism? The old age pensioner would never have obtained that extra $10. How is this going to work out? Across this nation today the young Liberals are talking about a republic for Canada. We stand against that, and many over on the other side stand against it as well, although there are some over there who seem to enjoy the favour of the Government, who talk about abolishing the Queen. What would happen if they were to move to abolish the Monarchy and then say, you are going to have a few hours to talk about it? The party whip works. This is a most controversial issue upon which Parliament should not be gagged. Read the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of Borden. I am not going to put them on Hansard again. Did all the wisdom of Parliament begin when these people took office?
Well, Mr. Speaker, these are things that must be considered. Overhanging us is supposed to be the sword of Damocles, an election, unless we bend. There are enough benders sitting over there who have bent to every wind. If a permanent Speaker were appointed, there would be no question but that there should be no appeals from the rulings of the Speaker. I ask you this, put in another man as Speaker such as we had in 1956, one who was the anointed of the Liberal Party, and see what would happen. He ruled us out, and he got instructions from over there. They cannot deny it, because the night before he
May 20, 1965

made the ruling that yesterday was not yesterday, but tomorrow or the reverse, somebody was out at Kingsmere and saw the Ministers' cars there. Mind you, they were only there for a visit, Mr. Speaker. They did not allow themselves, even by osmosis, to let the Speaker know what they were thinking about, but he certainly caught the idea.
I do not like to see appeals from Speakers' rulings. However, let us get a Speaker who will be entirely removed from and above the hurly-burly of politics or any consideration. They talk about appeals. The Prime Minister put on the record the number of appeals. He said that between 1867 and 1905 there were no appeals; between 1905 and 1931 there were 17; between 1931 and 1957, there were 89; 1956 to 1962, there were 3; 1962 to 1963, there were 6; 1963, 12 and 1964, 11. I took the trouble to ask a member of my staif to look up these appeals. He found that the appeals from Speaker's rulings in the year 1963 amounted to 5 from the Creditistes, 4 from the Progressive Conservatives and 2 from the N.D.P. We solve this immediately by abolishing appeals. If we had given up the right of appeal, what would have happened to us during the days of 1956, if another person, not cast in the mould of what Speakers should be were to occupy that place and make rulings such as he made: "I cannot hear you; I cannot see you."
Now, the difficulty in this connection will be removed by the appointment of a permanent Speaker. On the question of closure, it is amazing to note the change. As my hon. friend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) said, the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) was sitting over here at that time. What did the Prime Minister say about closure on March 16, 1962? Regarding the setting up of a committee in connection with it he said he believed that in the light of the experience of the past, the principle of closure need no longer be expected to need reform. That is what they said in opposition, and then they gave us a flag by closure.

They do not want to have this type of closure because they think there is going to be trouble, so they produce a refined variety, a civilized form, which will completely carry out the desires of the Government, and the number of bureaucrats that are in the Government. Today some of the highest bureaucrats try to determine policy, and believe we should do what they have in mind because it is good for us. They
House of Commons Procedures have this new plan evolved. I ask you to look up Quintin Hogg's book in which he deals with this question. This is a refined system and he says it is a very bad system. They have it in the United Kingdom, but they have it surrounded by protection for the opposition. There is no protection here. You can just imagine-no, I cannot imagine the Minister of Transport doing it because he knows parliament and he knows history. However, I can think of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). Would he not like to rise in his place and say, I am introducing this today and we are going to close up tonight, or whenever we get a day to debate it? Then, that is the end of it. In the United Kingdom, they protect the rights of parliament through a non-political and non-partisan Speaker, and there is no connotation of the present Speaker in that statement. I want to make that clear again.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The Business Committee will meet and it must be unanimous. This has been one of the weaknesses of Parliament since this Government gave third parties an official position by paying their leaders $4,000 and placing them in a position of equality within the House. Admirable though their conduct may be, that is a denial of parliament and I said so at the time. What is the reason parliament takes so long? Well, Mr. Speaker, the Government speaks on a matter, I speak, or whoever is acting for the Leader of the Opposition, and down you go. That does not happen in the U.K. parliament. Third parties that are not the alternative to the government are not placed in a position of equality.
When there is disagreement among the Business Committee, then the Government moves for an order allocating time for the item of business, and that is to be debatable for one day. This is a particularly formidable form of selective closure. It has been described in the Globe and Mail cartoon as, "Mcllraith's Capital Closure Kit;" and that is what it is.
This is dangerous. This represents a complete victory for the Government any time they want to rise, if they have the necessary allies to stand with them. What they don't want to hear, they won't hear. In the United Kingdom the Speaker stands as the custodian of the rights of minorities in the House and he does not allow closure to be applied unless within circumscribed limits. This, carried intc effect in its present form, is a design to prevent full discussion of controversial proposals.

Who would benefit? Well, it will benefit the cabinet, and the cabinet has become all powerful since 1914. Year by year in two world wars the cabinet became very powerful, and all experience has shown that the pathways of experiment become the highways of permanence. That is what has happened.
This will make parliament a rubber stamp of the government and the bureaucrats. If we had the protection of a non-partisan Speaker I would not argue the question as I am, but today, on the face of it, in this place every one of us is in the position of not being able to speak for whatever period he wants. In the United Kingdom this form of closure is not applied until after debate gets bogged down. Here they are going to be able to apply it any time, even before debate starts.
The Prime Minister says he hopes it will not be used very often. That is the excuse that goes back through the ages, "Just give us this power so that we will have it, and we assure you there will be no tyranny in its application." Mr. Speaker, unless there are safeguards this section, giving the cabinet or any minister the right at any time to say- I do not like to use the expression-to say "Shut up," with the support of those who will stand with the government, come what may, will make a puppet of parliament, will make parliament a puppet of cabinet. I say that we should not be called upon to agree, as we are, to certain portions of the resolution that is before us, to agree to accept it in whole, not turning it down. I say that this whole question should be submitted to a committee of parliament to consider the manner in which it will be surrounded by safeguards so that parliament will not, in a moment of weakness, abdicate its right to hear and be heard.
I do not know how many of the hon. members sitting over there have the attributes of the Government of 1956. None of them has ever disavowed it. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker; they don't want to hear us. They have a highly controversial question of legislation and they say to the House of Commons, "We don't want to hear you on this." If that had been in effect, where would the pension plan have been? Where would have been all the other changes that have been effected?
I make this closing appeal to the Government, but I will have more to say when the next resolution comes up. I make this appeal. Hon. Members opposite, you love this institution as I love it. Power corrupts. It has always been so. Lord Acton said absolute power corrupts absolutely.

Give the government of the day the power asked here, and no tyrant could ask for more. Mr. Speaker, I make an appeal to the Government, and I will make it direct to the Prime Minister-don't destroy this institution and its independence by making parliament a puppet at the whim of ministers who, directed by bureaucrats who like short cuts, want to force through controversial things however dangerous they may be to the whole field of human freedom within our land. I make that appeal. I do not suppose it will do other than fall on rocky soil, but there are parliamentarians over there. There are private Members who I would like to see speak upon this.
Why not make this is a matter of a free vote? Take off the whip. All of us want to see parliament made the great instrument of freedom. All of us are proud to be Members of Parliament. When I hear Members criticized and politics disdained, I have that feeling that you and I have, that all of us have. They can pour contempt upon those of us in public life, but no teaching of the church, no finding in science, no discovery in medicine, no new foundations in economics can be translated into action for the benefit of the people except through the often criticized politician. And I make this appeal: Don't trample on parliament for the sake of so-called efficiency.
Efficiency that is bought by the denial of the rights of the minority is a principle foreign to Canadian Confederation and a denial of all those things for which Macdonald, and Cartier, and Laurier, and King, and St. Laurent, and all the other Prime Ministers stood.

That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House a copy of all letters and other documents since the 1st day of January, 1964, exchanged between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States in connection with the Agreement providing for duty-free trade within the automobile industry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion which is now before the House I would first like to say that on the last day it came before the House, May 5, I asked for the yeas and nays of the House with regard to my request of the Government that the documents exchanged with the U.S. Government be produced. However, due to a procedural arrangement the vote that was held was on the Speaker's ruling and not on whether this information should be supplied to the House. At that time the Minister asked that this motion be transferred for debate, and so we find ourselves in this position today.
The reason I asked for this information was that I sincerely felt the people of Canada and the Members of this House should have been well informed as to the steps that had been taken with respect to the signing by Canada and the United States of this very important treaty. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that it was signed before ever being brought before this House for discussion. The Members of this House were never informed of any of
Canada-U.S. Automobile Agreement the particulars of this very complex subject. Parliament had been circumvented. The matter was introduced by Order in Council, and one of those abuses of power about which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) warned us in the very eloquent address just finished, was used.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the people are entitled to know more about this treaty, and it is of serious concern to the people of Canada that we have all the information possible presented to this House. In order to develop my reasoning in this regard I would like to place my remarks before the House under three headings. First, what material and information has been made available to the Congressmen of the United States? Second, what do we, as Members of the Canadian Parliament, know, and what information were we supplied with respecting the signing of this treaty? Third, what are some of the steps that have been taken to supply information in previous treaties which have been signed between these two great countries?
Let us look for a minute at the information given to Congressmen in the United States with respect to this matter. Six days after the signing in the United States there was tabled in the Congressional Record of January 22 an item entitled "United States-Canadian trade in automotive products". Let us see what can be found in this Congressional Record, which corresponds to our Hansard in Canada. First of all it outlines the whole agreement that was signed by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson), together with a statement describing in detail the background to this agreement. Second, we find statements that were made about the agreement by the President of General Motors Corporation, Mr. Donner; Mr. Henry Ford II, Chairman of the Board of Ford Motor Company; Mr. Townsend, President of Chrysler Corporation; the President of American Motors Corporation, and Mr. Reuther, President of United Auto Workers. We also find several editorial comments. We even find the exchange which took place between President Johnson and the Prime Minister of Canada on the signing of this treaty at President Johnson's farm in Texas. I should like to read one or two of the exchanges between the two leaders. It says;
The President: Mr. Prime Minister would you like to make some observations and answer questions before you leave?
May 20, 1965

Canada-U.S. Automobile Agreement
Then a very interesting question was put to the Prime Minister:
Mr. Prime Minister, why could not this agreement be used as a basis for other agreements in other industries?
That is the very question I put to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) today. The Prime Minister answered:
Well as far as we are concerned we would like to explore that possibility. This agreement may be important not only in itself but it could be important from that point of view. But the automotive industry, the organization of it on this continent, lends itself to this kind of agreement more easily than other industries. But we will certainly be anxious to have a look at the other situations to see if we can apply this. Anyway, we made a start.
As we read through this report we find out all this background and what happened at the meeting between the Prime Minister and the President of the United States. This was prior to the last meeting they had at Temple University in Philadelphia, which was not quite as friendly a meeting. Then there is the report of the hearing before a United States Senate subcommittee. The proceedings are all printed for us to read; but if we want to know any of these things, as Canadian Parliamentarians, we have to write to the United States to find out what happened. This report of the subcommittee of the Committee on Foreign Relations, of February 10 last lists the officials attending the meeting. They were Hon. G. Griffith Johnson, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, accompanied by Robert L. McNeill, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Trade Policy, and Julius L. Katz, Deputy Director, Office of International Trade, Department of State. These men were there and discussed U.S. countervailing duties versus remission plan, the United States-Canadian employment level affected by the agreement, and so on. All these subjects were discussed by this group. There is a rather interesting section here:
Naturally, Canada wants to be sure that the Canadian automotive industry will participate in this growth. Therefore, Canada has asked each of the Canadian producers for a statement of their intentions for expansion of their production in Canada.
Senator Symington: Will their reply be a matter of public record?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

They are not now a matter of public record. We did not participate, of course, in negotiations and we are not familiar with the contents of the arrangements between each company and the Canadian Government. So that I am not in a position to answer that question, Senator.
Senator Symington: Will they be a matter of public record?

I would suppose this would be a matter for decision of the Canadian Government and the companies. It would not be something which we would have any say in.
Senator Symington: Well, then, could I ask, respectfully, why that is included in this statement?
I just mention this very hurriedly and briefly, Mr. Speaker, to bring to the attention of the House some of these matters which have been discussed by Congressmen. On the other hand, what do we in Canada know about it and what have we been told? We have been treated as a bunch of babes in the woods, as far as being told anything about this great treaty which has been signed.
A news release was issued by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) on January 15, not for release until 6.00 p.m. that day, which was the day before the treaty was signed in the United States. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, the House was in recess at the time. To my knowledge-I think this is true-this press release was sent to the Ottawa addresses of hon. Members, and I do not suppose that too many of us saw it until the House reconvened. This news release and a copy of the agreement was not tabled in this House until February 24; the Minister can correct me if I am wrong about that. This treaty was signed on January 16; yet it was not until February 24 that the agreement was tabled in the House. Along with the copy of the agreement were certain exhibits, as well as the motor vehicles tariff order. This is couched in language which is most difficult for laymen to understand, and to illustrate my point I should like to read one part of it which deals with the ratio of the net sales value. It says:
(A)	the ratio of the net sales value of which to the net sales value of all vehicles of that class sold for consumption in Canada by the manufacturer in that period is equal to or higher than the ratio of the net sales value of all vehicles of that class produced in Canada by the manufacturer in the base year to the net sales value of all vehicles of that class sold for consumption in Canada by the manufacturer in the base year, and is not in any case lower than seventy-five to one hundred, and
(B)	the Canadian value added of which is equal to or greater than the Canadian value added of all vehicles of that class produced in Canada by the manufacturer in the base year;
To understand what I have just quoted one would have to be a Philadelphia lawyer, because it is just about as complicated as it could be. However, as I say, we were supplied with a copy of this agreement on February 24.
As I mentioned earlier, this treaty was approved by Order in Council instead of by

debate on a resolution presented to the House. We are told that we are going to have the chance to debate a resolution which will be put on the order paper, but it is not there yet. This treaty was signed on January 16 and as yet we have had no chance to debate it, and I ask why. I maintain the answer to this question is that the Government is afraid to bring the matter before the House until the treaty is approved by the Congress of the United States. I am convinced that is the reason for the delay. As far as I can see there is no mention of the manufacturers' statement of intention in this agreement.
On April 5 I asked about these letters. We had to ask because the Minister did not see fit to table the letters or statement of intention of the manufacturers, and did not do so until April 26. I appreciate this House was in recess from April 14 to 26, but these documents could have been tabled before April 14, which was nine days after they were first asked for. Why the delay in tabling them, Mr. Speaker? I do not know. This is information which we parliamentarians should have been supplied with; and I have endeavoured to show that United States Congressmen were supplied with far more material than we were supplied with.
There have been other treaties signed by Canada and the United States, and in those cases there has been tabled the exchange of notes and other information. Let me refer to the Columbia River Treaty, for example.
I see no difference between this treaty with that one. No security is involved in the automobile treaty with the United States. I have before me the exchange of notes between Canada and the United States of America dated May 25, 1964 having to do with a continental radar system. I also have the exchange of notes between Canada and the United States on boundary waters and seaway tolls dated June 30, 1964.
I have tried to give reasons, Mr. Speaker, for asking for this information, and to give the background to establish why I felt I was within my rights in so doing. On behalf of the Members of this House and the people of Canada I ask the Minister to table all the correspondence between Canada and the United States with respect to the Canada-United States automobile treaty.

There have been a number of exchanges of views about the agreement in this House, and hon. Moreover, the Ministers have stated that there will be an opportunity for a full debate and for this House to approve of this automotive agreement before the conclusion of the exchange of notes which is required to bring it into force.
The documents for which the hon. Member for Wellington South has asked are actually working papers relating to successive drafts of the Canada-United States automotive agreement. This Government is proud of the agreement and of the work performed during the lengthy negotiations which led up to it. Canadian economic interests were of prime consideration at all times. The hon. Member then asks: Why not table these preliminary documents? The answer to his question is simply that to do so, however politically convenient this might appear to be in the short run, it would clearly be a departure from normal diplomatic practice, would hamper negotiations in respect of other subjects and would be against Canada's long term interest.
I do not think the Canada-United States working papers would contribute very much to the information of the hon. Member in his quest for more understanding of this agreement. In fact, in some ways they would be misleading because they probably would be disjointed. Kept secret would be some of the highly privileged information resulting from conversations which is related to this whole matter.
As I am sure the hon. Member for Wellington South appreciates, these negotiations were not conducted primarily by exchanges of correspondence, or letters, as he suggests.

DEBATES	May	20 1965
They took place in a series of half a dozen or more confidential meetings between the senior officials of our Government and of the Government of the United States. Naturally drafts, partial drafts and working papers were exchanged on such occasions, but they would mean very little to the hon. Member, were they to be made public. During these meetings there was always oral give and take. This went on over the course of several months. There were not very many documents actually exchanged at these meetings, and I assure the hon. Member that they would be rather disjointed and misleading in the light of the totality of the negotiations.
I turn now to the customary practice as far as making public such privileged documents is concerned. The House has from time to time been faced with the reservation that certain papers exchanged with other governments during the course of international negotiations could not be made public on the ground that to do so would be contrary to diplomatic practice. This is a reasonable reservation which Members of this House have in the past been able to accept. It has not, in fact, been invoked often since it would appear that Members have seldom requested the disclosure of such highly confidential inter-government exchanges.
In my experience, Mr. Speaker, when it has been given as grounds for not tabling such material, the House has accepted the explanation and has not pressed the matter further. Several such instances come to mind. On May 5, for instance, the hon. Member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) was prepared to modify his motion for this reason. I also recollect other similar cases; for example, in October, 1963 when we had a motion calling for correspondence between Canada and the United States concerning wheat sales to the U.S.S.R. and other countries, and in April of last year in connection with papers relating to negotiation of the Columbia River Treaty. On rare occasions the Government may have offered to approach another country to ask for permission to publish such material, but when it has done so, permission has almost invariably been refused until many years after the event when, in the normal course, diplomatic correspondence often enters the public historical record.
Relations between Governments have to be conducted, if they are to be effective, in accordance with certain simple ground rules.
May 20, 1965

Among friendly nations a respect by each country for the other's confidences is a prime requisite in the conduct of foreign policy. All Governments treat correspondence of this kind as privileged and, in addition to the the precedents in this House which I have cited, there are numerous similar examples of legislatures in other countries accepting the position I have outlined.
Before negotiations on as complex a matter as the Canada-United States automotive agreement can begin, each Government must decide both on its objectives and on the extent to which it is prepared to adapt these in the light of negotiations which are to follow. During the course of such negotiations there must inevitably be a good deal of give and take; positions are modified; Governments have to be consulted from time to time, and certain drafts have to be exchanged. But if the representatives either of Canada or any other Government expected that such preliminary exchanges were likely to be made public in the future their entire approach would be very different. It would be more formal and, indeed, less flexible. The whole process of negotiation would therefore be more difficult and fruitful results less likely.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Thus the public interest requires that the Government of Canada, or for that matter any Government, negotiate on the basis that preliminary exchanges will not be published. Moreover, in the case of the automotive agreement it was not contemplated that the preliminary exchanges between our Government and the Government of the United States would be published. To do so at this stage would not only violate customary diplomatic usage but would create an important and, indeed, unfortunate precedent which other countries would have to bear in mind when dealing with Canada in the future. Their attitudes toward negotiations with us might well be altered to our disadvantage in the sense that our negotiating partners would be less forthcoming and less co-operative.
I think I have dealt with the hon. Member's motion as fairly as I could. I recognize his general interest in the automotive agreement. His numerous questions and his present motion are testimony to this fact. I also respect his desire to be well informed about the intricacies of the agreement. before the realization of this agreement, one must recognize this is a type of agreement that is quite new, quite far reaching in its value with regard to setting a precedent for further developments along this line in the future. Certainly it will be of vital importance to our nation if we are to move away from the protectionist economy that has been our mode of living in Canada for the first 97 years of our existence as a nation. A low tariff or free trade economy is unexplored territory so far as Canada is concerned.
Those of us who live in the extremities of Canada, of course, are in a position where we have suffered economically from the effects of high tariffs in Canada. As a consequence of this, too much trade has been strictly within the nation. We watch with interest and applaud any move toward freer trade, and toward a greater international exchange of goods with economies of size, and the benefit from the new trade that can be obtained therein.
Now, having said that we are in favour of a lower tariff arrangement, I think that this agreement, from what we know of it at the present time, indicates an arrangement that gives us the best of all possible worlds. We not only move toward lower tariffs or freer trade in this important field of automotive production, but at the same time we have an arrangement that protects our workers and our industries in this country. I would be the first to grant that we can never achieve any free trade or lower tariff arrangement of any consequence in Canada, any success in the Kennedy round, the GATT talks or any improvement in international trade conditions, without some dislocation. There are bound to be some people who may have to change positions, or the type of work they have been doing, or their location. Surely no treaty for the reduction of a tariff or for free trade can be achieved unless there are benefits for both parties. I cannot imagine, Mr. Speaker, a situation in which two countries would sign an agreement if there were not some benefits to each side. What is good for General Motors.

My hon. friend says, what is good for General Motors. There is a lot more involved than General Motors; and without going far afield from the subject under consideration I would point out to him that Studebaker, which manufactures only in Canada today, stands to benefit from this treaty, and that Volvo, who are manufacturing in my constituency, would benefit very substantially by having the American market open to them as soon as they are able to achieve 50 per cent Canadian content in their production.
Returning to the consideration of whether the papers themselves should be produced, one must consider the disadvantages, that future negotiations would be hampered, that governments dealing with a government operating under a system whereby all confidential papers of this nature are produced would be hesitant in future. We also have the fact that when these negotiations were taking place the American officials participating in them must surely have presumed
[Mr. ReganJ
they were of a secret nature, must have presumed that the practice which existed in the past as regards papers of this type not being produced would be followed. Surely it would not be honourable for this Government to break with the precedent of the past and produce such papers, if the negotiating parties had depended upon the fact that what had always been the practice in past negotiations would occur on this occasion.
In our system of responsible government it is up to the administration of the day to carry on such negotiations and to enter into such treaties or agreements if the government considers it in the best interests of the country. Then eventually the matter comes back to Parliament, as the House has been told will be done in this case.
If these papers were made available we would have a situation wherein opposition Members in both Canada and the U.S. would peruse them carefully, to try and pinpoint any areas within the over-all agreement which were disadvantageous to their respective countries. If they did so, then of course Government Members in Canada and government supporters in the U.S. would have to deal at greater length with the respective areas of advantage, and very shortly what was being said by Government Members in dealing with the details of the negotiations in this country, from information gleaned from those papers, would be utilized in the United States by those opposed to the agreement, and vice versa. Therefore the possibility of achieving these worth-while types of reduction in tariffs in order to move toward freer trade would be greatly hindered.
That being the case I think that acceptance of the motion moved by the hon. Member for Wellington South, which I think exhibits his true and genuine concern to obtain more information on the subject, would be ill-advised. From the remarks he made one might conclude that he was concerned, not so much with what may be in these papers as in having a better understanding of the agreement, and this applies to the hon. Member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) also.
While patience is a virtue that those of us who are elected representatives of the people do not always have in large measure, surely in this instance the hon. Member, having regard to the undertakings he has heard from the treasury benches, that ample and effective measures will be taken to

offset any dislocations that occur; that the over-all agreement is beneficial to Canada; having regard to the undertakings given by the industry that an over-all increase of a very substantial nature will occur for Canada; having regard to the fact that there is to be a debate in due course on this matter, should feel it would be in the best interests of all concerned, and indeed of his country, to withdraw the motion and be happy that we have an administration which will take care of the interests of the industry and the workers.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have but little time to participate in this important debate as I have many important contributions to make; but in the first place I would like to point out to the House that the very proper stand taken by the Minister in refusing to produce these papers is in the highest traditions of this party, to the effect that we live up to our international commitments.
That cannot be said of all parties; but I would point out that in the negotiations which preceded the treaty and the agreement there was an understanding, there was confidence, between the parties that these prior negotiations, these prior exchanges of correspondence were of a confidential nature. As I said earlier, we live up to such international understandings, be they explicit or tacit, as they were in this particular case.
We are not known as a party that gets into trouble with our international friends and neighbours either by disclosing agreements which are understood to be secret, or failing to live up to commitments, or by producing documents, forged or otherwise, which might get us into international involvements with our good friends and neighbours. May 20. 1965

House of Commons Procedures

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1.	That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 36 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions "That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair"; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year. That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-two members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follow;
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thoroughly agree with those who say that parliament is not just a club of good fellows who should indulge in a few niceties, pass a few laws, bring the session to an end and go home. Parliament is a place of contention, of debate, of attack and counter-attack, of cut and thrust. Experience has shown that this is the best way to get a full examination of the matters that concern a democratic nation like Canada.
When we discuss parliamentary reform, whatever changes we may be proposing, none of us proposes that there be curtailment of or interference with freedom of speech and freedom of debate. There are many passages one could quote in support of this position, but I am sure that all of them are to be found on the pages of Hansard and I will not take the time of the House or my time to quote them again tonight. It is also true that the whole study of parliamentary procedure over the years, indeed over the decades, has been an endeavour to find a balance between the right to speak at as much length as seems desirable, and the right of parliament to make decisions.
It is in the attempt to find a balance between these two goals that many parliaments before this one have worked out rules and have amended them from time to time. The rule changes that have taken place since I have had the honour of being a Member of this House of Commons have been in that vein. I think particularly of the rather complete overhaul that we made in 1955, when we endeavoured to maintain the right of as much speech as seemed necessary, but also when we tried to establish certain limitations on the length of debate so that parliament might have a chance to make decisions.
May 20, 1965

We of the New Democratic Party have felt for a long time that an overhaul such as was made in 1955 needs to be made again. We are not new converts to the idea of allocating time, of planning the parliamentary year. This is something we have advocated for a considerable time. I have before me a document of which some Members will be cognizant, namely a press release that was put out by the leader of this party on September 22, 1964, in which there were set out ten proposals that we made for the reform of parliament. In the main they proposed that we try to make better use of the time that we have within a calendar year. I also have before me a number of documents that I will not even pick up; modesty prevents me from so doing. They are speeches I have made and letters and articles I have written for the press in which I have personally argued very strongly that parliament consider the advisability, the necessity of planning the best use of our time. I have pointed out on many occasions that the sheer increase in the volume of business with which we must deal since Canada came into being nearly 100 years ago makes it impossible for us to carry on with the kind of rules, so far as time is concerned, that were adequate in 1867.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we of the New Democratic Party are in support of the principle contained in the resolution we are now debating. In saying that, I refer in particular to the resolution which is known as order No. 14 on the order paper, which is what is now before us. I distinguish between order No. 14 and order No. 15, which is to come later, because order No. 15 has in it a number of details which we feel should be modified, changed or even dropped altogether. We even have some changes that we think should be made in order No. 14, the resolution that we are now discussing. But in so far as it proposes that we grapple with this question of the proper use of our parliamentary time, we are in support of the principle of this resolution.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We urge the House to take this resolution and the principle behind it very seriously. We think that one of the problems which confronts us in Parliament is to do just that. We were all impressed by the oratory of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his speech this afternoon. We were impressed with his appeal at the conclusion of his remarks when he urged that we do not 22620-99
House of Commons Procedures destroy parliament. He said that if we interfered too drastically with the freedom of speech as he defined it, we would be doing just that.
We of this party, Mr. Speaker, make the same appeal: Do not destroy parliament, but do not destroy it by failing to modernize our rules, by leaving us in the kind of situation where by endless talk on one, two or three issues, we prevent parliament from getting at a host of other issues which demand our attention. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we are in support of the principle of the resolution moved in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) which is now before us.
At this point there are two things that I should like to say to the Opposition side of the House, and there are two things I should like to say following that to the Government side. When I address myself to the Opposition side of the House I have in mind all of us who sit on this side. I would remind the Leader of the Opposition that there are 40 of us in this corner of the chamber. We represent more than 25 per cent of the votes of the people of Canada cast during the last two elections, and it is not likely that the people of Canada would want to see us sloughed off in the way he suggested this afternoon. However I merely say that in addressing myself to the Opposition side of the House I am addressing my remarks to all of us who sit to Mr. Speaker's left.
The first thing I want to say is, perhaps, a repetition or the placing of emphasis on what I have already said, namely this: Let us on the Opposition side of the House realize that arrangements for the limitation of debate, arrangements for the allocation of time, are not to be shouted down by calling them closure. Methods whereby debate is limited, whereby debate comes to an end at a certain time, are not nearly as serious a form of closure as is the situation we are faced with when, by endless talk on one or two subjects, the opportunity to get at other subjects is completely foreclosed. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is in the interests of those of us on the Opposition side of the House that there be planning of our time so that we can get at all of the items that are before parliament-all of the matters of business that demand our attention.
