speechtext:
If time permitted, Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to quote again Sir Wilfrid Laurier and other great men of the past, the giants of our Parliament and the giants of Westminster, who have suggested that posterity blesses the pertinacity of those who stand firm to prevent something being done which ought not to be done. I could

quote other authorities but I will not have the time to do so. I could quote Sir Charles Tupper's farewell letter to the Conservative party when he was leaving its leadership in 1901.
It is also our job on the Opposition side of the House to try to get things out of the Government and to try to get Parliament to do things. I submit that when we on the Opposition side go on the hustings in an election campaign we spend some of our time, yes, telling the people what we did to try and stop the Government from doing this, that and the other thing; but I submit we spend most of the time telling the people what we got out of the Government, telling the people of the things we fought for.
I submit that that is just as important a role, so far as the Opposition is concerned, as is the role of opposing. Our job, to quote Sir Charles Tupper, is to advance those things which the administration neglects to advance. Therefore we should not ask for rules to be left in such a way that all we do is oppose and use endless time-I use that word again -to oppose things, because part of our job is to see to it that we get things done for the people of Canada whom we represent.
I said I wanted to say a couple of things to the Government as well, Mr. Speaker; and by "Government" in this instance I mean all those to Mr. Speaker's right who support the Government of the day. The first thing I want to say is this, and I say it very strongly to the Government: Do not go too far with this proposition. Do not take the principle that parliament must get things done as the only principle on which parliament must operate. We are a democracy. A democracy consists not just in universal suffrage, not just in the right of the people to vote for the government of their choice; democracy includes respect for the rights of minorities.
This is expressed in parliament by giving to the opposition a right that is almost the equal of the right of the government. In fact, the only right the government has which the opposition does not have is the right that flows from the fact that it has a majority.
I know that in this Parliament we have a Government that is technically in a minority position; but it has carried on for over two years, so in one way or another it finds itself in the kind of majority position which a government needs in order to carry on. But the minute that a government devises rules which give to it the complete, the sole and final control of the business of the House,
May 20, 1965	COMMONS
it is negating the basic principle of democracy, namely that minorities-that the opposition-has rights.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am going to come in a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to some of the details of what is being proposed, but I do want to assert the basic principle, which has been part of our parliamentary thinking over the years, that no government must ever take unto itself the complete and final control of Parliament. Neither should the Opposition, but it is not able to do so. If the Government does that, it moves in the direction of dictatorship. I assert that it is just as much in the interest of Parliament as it is in the interests of those who happen to sit to the left of Mr. Speaker that the rights of all the Members of this House be protected. I urge that this be kept in mind when providing for new rules, and that the convenience of the Government in the obtaining of decisions be not the end all of proposals that are placed before the House.
The second thing I wish to say to the Government is this. In all probability the kind of rules now proposed will be endorsed, at least in principle, if not in detail. They will be adopted by this House, and when they are the Government is going to lose something it now has. It is going to lose the excuse that it has forever been able to fall back on, that it cannot get certain items of business through the House because of an insufficiency of time. When these new rules are passed, and the business of the House can be dealt with more expeditiously, there will be time to deal with all these social security measures the Prime Minister talked about the other day. Things like medicare will not be capable of being put off for another 40 years after these rules have been changed. The problems in respect of doing our* part in external aid, education and finance will not be capable of being put off by the Government, simply by saying that the processes of parliament take up too much time.
I asked the Prime Minister a day or two ago about the 30 or more items contained in the Speech from the Throne, and whether we were going to get to them this session.
I received the usual answer to that question, that the Government would try to bring them forward as quickly as possible. It has been traditional in this place that Speeches from the Throne contain a great many things with which we never deal. Many of these 22620-99J
DEBATES	1533
House of Commons Procedures things are nothing more than window dressings, but are never brought before the House because of a suggested lack of time.
Let me suggest to this Government that when these rules are passed the Government is going to have time to accomplish those things set out in throne speeches, and we will then have the right to insist that they be accomplished. The excuse of insufficient time will then no longer be capable of use, because these rules will in effect provide the Government with sufficient time. We can then expect the Government to proceed with those things mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. We will then expect action in the solution of these many problems which the Government itself says are demanding attention.
Having said these things of a general character, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to say something specific about the procedural resolutions now before us. The next resolution on the order paper to be considered is No. 15. Only two people have so far taken part in this debate with respect to item No. 14, but the comments of those two individuals have ranged widely over the subjects contained in items 14 and 15. I should like at this time to make a passing reference to item 15, although I might say that for the most part we intend to debate the resolution set out in order No. 15 at a later date.
May I now say a few words about some of the details contained in order No. 14. There is a proposal that the debate on supply in the House of Commons be limited to 36 days. In line with the statements I have already made, we accept the principle that there should be a time limit on the number of days to be spent on the debate in respect of supply in the House of Commons. We agree with the proposal of the Prime Minister in this resolution that the estimates should be referred to standing committees. We also agree that, having done this, certainly less time ought to be needed in the House of Commons itself in this regard. We do think, however, that the Government has gone too far in proposing that the time limit be 36 days and that there be included, for the purposes of the supply debate limited to 36 days, four categories of business, namely the motions that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair, which can take up to 12 days, supplementary estimates, interim supply and the main estimates.
In the proposals which have previously been made regarding the limitation of time with respect to estimates, for example, the
May 20. 1965

House of Commons Procedures report which the committee made last session, the limitation was suggested only with respect to the debate on the main estimates. The proposal made last year by the committee added up to a limit of 45 days with respect to the main estimates. I do not mind the Government cutting the time from 45 days down to 36 days, provided this limit refers only to the main estimates; but the resolution now before us includes also not only the 12 days of debate on the motions that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair, which involves really a number of want of confidence motions, but also interim supply and supplementary estimates.
We propose to move a compromise, as an indication of our willingness to go along with the principle of this resolution, in the form of an amendment that the 36 day limit be applicable only to two of the four categories, namely interim supply and the main estimates. We believe that it is fair to include interim supply in this limitation because, after all, that is part of what is included in the main estimates. We do not think it is fair to include the supplementary estimates, which may include things entirely foreign to that which is included in the main estimates. Nor do we think it is fair to include the 12 days of debate on the motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair. This is the kind of change we feel ought to be made in the proposal regarding the limitation of time on estimates.
We welcome the suggestion that this proposal be referred to a special committee of 22 which will be asked to work out the details, having in mind the rights of the Opposition and various other details. We intend to make certain proposals in that regard at the time the special committee of 22 is studying this proposal.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps this is not the usual time, in the middle of one's speech, but I should like to move an amendment, and I should like to do it now, since it is related to the remarks I have just made. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That the resolution be amended by deleting from paragraph 1 thereof the sentence which reads: "For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions 'That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair'; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year"; and by substituting thereof the following sentence: "For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of interim supply and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year".

It is our hope that this amendment will commend itself not only to Members of the Opposition, but to Members of the Government, or that if not acceptable in this form to the Government, the Government will propose some alternative or compromise. Surely this is a detail in respect of which we can get together.
I should now like to say-

At this time I wish to make one or two comments about the proposal with respect to Standing Order 15A, regarding the establishment of a Business Committee. Obviously in principle we will support this suggestion. As a party we have been arguing for this for some time. During the last session I had

the privilege of being the Chairman of a subcommittee of the Committee on Procedure and Organization. That committee was unanimous in its support of a proposal for a time allocation rule which was not quite as severe or strict as the one now before us. I suggest that it might have been advantageous to accept that proposal last session. But at any rate we favour this idea in principle. However, we think there are some aspects of the proposed standing order 15A that have to be clarified, and we think there are one or two places where changes ought to be made. I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) a question yesterday at the end of his speech about the meaning of subparagraph 2 with particular regard to whether or not the reference to the Business Committee of an item or stage meant the whole gamut of a piece of legislation or just one stage. To my surprise his answer was that it meant either. In other words, it could be one stage such as second reading, or it could be the whole gamut. I think that is a mistake.
I should like to see this Business Committee work. I come at it critically but I come at it sympathetically. I think this is a good idea but I think that the chances of this proposition working are diminished if when the Business Committee meets it is faced, not with just how long we will spend on second reading but how long we will spend on second reading, Committee of the Whole and third reading, even when that far in advance we do not know what may be involved. I think that this good idea-of course it is a good idea; some of us have advocated it-would work better if one stage at a time were referred to the Business Committee.
Another point I want to comment on has to do with subparagraph 5 of the proposed standing order 15A.

speechtext:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the concept the Minister has of this order is that it is going to work that way and that we are going to have to bring it into play on every piece of legislation and have all these debates, the order is not going to work. We have got along in some respects on the basis of agreement among the House Leaders, and I see this Business Committee as one that will meet fairly often. It will frequently reach agreement without having to report to the House and it is only in cases where there is difficulty, in cases where endless debate is looming or where there is undue contention, that this method will be brought into play.
I think that the value of this kind of order is diminished if the Government drafts it in such a way that it puts into its own hands what amounts to almost complete and ultimate control. I think it should be drafted with a view to its being the kind of order that will induce co-operation among the various parties in the House in trying to plan the business of the House and to plan the parliamentary year.
It is in that vein, Mr. Speaker, that we are particularly concerned about subparagraph 5 which provides what is to happen when there is not unanimous agreement on the part of those who make up the Business Committee. I take it from this paragraph that even if the Government were beaten 4 to 1 in the Business Committee, a Minister could still operate under subclause 5 of 15A. I recognize that there has to be provision for these things to be dealt with when there is not unanimity, and in the rule that my subcommittee drafted at the last session we tried to make provision as to what would happen if there was unanimity and what would happen if there was a majority decision but not unanimity. I think we were perhaps wise in going only that far. The rule of unanimity is perhaps too restrictive, but surely a rule that goes to the other extreme and allows a representative from the Business Committee who has been beaten 4 to 1 to come back to the House and still get his will is going a little bit too far.
May 20, 1965

House of Commons Procedures
The Prime Minister made a bit of a slip at one point yesterday when he told me that he thought this matter could be discussed by the special committee of 22 referred to in paragraph 1 of the resolution. I recognize that the Prime Minister made a mistake and that it does not read that way, but I should like to suggest that the Government reconsider this point and that it allow the special committee of 22 to take a look at the proposed standing order 15A, and in particular paragraph 5 of that order. I am not worried very much about the rest of it. I think the rest of it is pretty good. Any details on which we differ are minor, but certainly the position that the Government would take in circumstances where it has been beaten 4 to 1 in the Business Committee is one which I think ought to be reviewed.
One suggestion that our subcommittee made last year in one draft was that if there was not unanimity in the Business Committee the number of days that might be proposed in the House for limitation of a debate should be subject to the provision that on the last of those days the ten o'clock adjournment be lifted and the House be allowed to continue as long as necessary that night so that those who had speeches to make could make them. I might say, by the way, that this is the practice at Westminster which is so often held up to us as a model that we should follow.
There are other ways to deal with this problem. There could be a limitation on the number of days into which the Government could compress a debate. There are various other forms of protection that could be put into subparagraph 5 which, as I say, presents a serious difficulty because here is a case where the Government, having been beaten in the Business Committee 4 to 1, is still reserving the right to tell the House what it shall do. I recognize the precautions that are there. I recognize, for example, that a Minister, having been beaten in the Business Committee, cannot move a motion until the fourth day. The matter has to be referred to the Business Committee itself for three days and there has to be a report back, and even then the Minister has to give notice of a debate to take place at a later date. I realize, therefore, that what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said this afternoon, that a motion could be made and the matter could be all over in one day, just will not happen. The Minister tries to get something done on a Monday and it could

be the next Monday or Tuesday before subparagraph 5 is brought into full operation. I realize that this is a pretty serious step for a Government to take and that it may not be taken very often-I hope not. But the very fact that this provision is there is a threat which I suggest detracts from the attractiveness-I use that word advisedly-of a Business Committee, the studied effort of which should be to plan decently and effectively the business of the House.
So, Mr. Speaker, I make this plea, and in this respect I am not moving an amendment. I cannot because I have already moved one. As a supporter of the principle of time allocation I make the plea that a new look be taken at that aspect of the proposed standing order 15A.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) interrupted to ask me what I thought about one or two other things that bear on the other resolution that the Prime Minister will be moving. Obviously we should not be discussing it under this resolution, but both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have done so, so perhaps I might say a word or two-although I make it clear that the Members of this group will have more to say on that resolution when we get into Committee of the Whole on it, as we will.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
First may I say that both with respect to the resolution we are now discussing and with respect to the other one I think there was merit in the implication of the question asked yesterday by the hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) with regard to whether these changes were to be made absolutely permanent or subject to review. I think the Prime Minister was quite justified in saying that he did not want to make them temporary because he did not want the House to convey to the country that we do not know what we are doing. But I think the idea that came out of the Prime Minister's mouth, namely that provision might now be made for a review of these changes at the end of one or two sessions, is a good one. Mind you, if this Government stays in power all we need is a Government commitment that this will be done, but I think it might be better to have written into the resolution somewhere a provision that at the end of a certain period of time these new rules will be reviewed. I think I can say for Members generally that we are prepared to try more drastic rule changes than we would otherwise accept if there were the knowledge that we would
May 20, 1965

have a chance to review them later. These rules, while to me they are attractive because they are based on the general principle of planning our parliamentary year, nevertheless are sufficiently far reaching that there should be a provision for their review at a later time.
Now I should like to say a word or two about one or two items in the other resolution. We question the desirability or advisability of the lengthened hours. We do not think it is a case of simple mathematics, that is of adding up the number of hours you get in the longer week and dividing that by a number of days and saying you will save time. You will not save time that way. We believe that the period between six and eight in particular will be wasted. We feel also that the proposal to sit after ten o'clock at night, while acceptable in principle, needs to be altered. We quite agree that there have been many situations that were not desirable, where the whole House seemed to want to go on and finish something in 15 or 20 minutes, maybe even an hour some night and one Member could say, no, and that was it. However, we do not believe we should go to the other extreme and bring in a rule under which night after night at ten o'clock and Wednesday and Friday at six o'clock, it would be possible, provided there were not ten objectors, to bring in this kind of motion that would keep things going endlessly, as the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) would say. I think the rule should have in it certain restrictions to make it possible to go for no more than an hour unless unanimous consent were given, or that it should not be used more than once or twice a week. In other words, do not deal with the situation you are trying to solve by bringing in a rule of such sweeping application as this one.
Neither in order paper item No. 14 nor in order paper item No. 15 are there to be found two or three things that last session's committee recommended, which we think ought to be included. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) agreed with that proposition this afternoon. I think that the whole question
House of Commons Procedures of the proper allocation of our time includes the concept of making greater use of our committees. But we think, Mr. Speaker, that you will not get the best work done in committees if two, three, four or ten of them have to sit while the House is sitting. I submit, from my experience, that the committees that do the very best work are committees that do not have the distraction of having Members run from the committee room to the House of Commons. I think the proposal of last session's committee that there be a certain break was a good one. We were not wedded, and I am not wedded, to the particular timetable that was proposed. But we do believe that there should be periods when the House recesses so that the committees can meet and do their work.
In the same vein we urge that the Government give more consideration to the whole question of research facilities and assistance for Members of the House of Commons. I bring this in at this time because we are talking about improving the job that Members do, and giving more work to the committees is one way of doing it. It employs more Members in our work and it requires more Members to become familiar with the tasks that are around here. I think if Members are going to do this that there has to be faced this problem of there being some kind of opposition civil service, if you want to call it that. There has to be research assistance available so that Members can do a better job both in the House and in committees. I am extremely sorry that neither of these important subjects was mentioned in either of the resolutions brought forward by the Government, though they were subjects about which the special committee had something to say in a number of its reports.

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I think through some misunderstanding, this did not come within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works, and Mr. Speaker said:
Order. I am sure it would take considerable time to think up the proper words to apply to this significant question and occasion.
It is on that account I ask permission to raise the question this evening. I think there was some misunderstanding as to the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works and his interest in this subject, and I am sure when I asked the question the majority of the Members of the House thought I was dealing with a subject that was entirely within the responsibility and jurisdiction of provincial governments. However, that is not so. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I rarely ask a question that is not in order in accordance with the rules of the House.
I asked this question because I know of the interest of the Minister and his officials in promoting safe highway driving in Canada. I know of the work being done by the Minister's department to co-ordinate the ideas and proposals advanced by provincial highway safety councils and other groups. I know of the concern of the Canadian people, the R.C.M.P., provincial and municipal police forces with the rapidly increasing number of fatalities caused by highway accidents, and

I am very pleased to note that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works is listening very closely to what I have to say, and I am looking forward to his reply.
But before asking my final question I wish to bring to the attention of the House an editorial published in the Nelson Daily News of Thursday, May 6, 1965, which is a reprint of one published in the Vancouver Province, and I do so because I think it deals with very poor advice from persons who should know better, from their experience with respect to administration of highways and the administration of the law. The editorial is entitled "Invitation to Recklessness," and states:
Alberta Highways Minister Gordon Taylor has joined his B.C. counterpart, P. A. Gaglardi, in defending high speeds on highways; in fact he favours removing speed limits altogether.
Mr. Taylor and Mr. Gaglardi also agree that speed alone is not the worst danger on the road, but that "when liquor is added to speed it is a deadly killer."
At this point both gentlemen seem to abandon both common sense and the evidence of traffic control systems in many parts of North America.
For example, the New Jersey Turnpike, a freeway superior in engineering to most B.C. and Alberta highways, strictly enforces a speed limit of 60 miles per hour and boasts an accident record far below the national average.
Extensive traffic safety surveys have shown that highway deaths and injuries are uniformly less in areas where there are reasonable speed limits and intensive police patrolling.
And what is the point, after admitting that the combination of liquor and speed is the worst traffic killer, in advocating removal of speed limits?
[DOT] (10:00 pun.)
With weapons ranging from Carrie Nation's hatchet to national prohibition, people have tried -and failed-to stamp out excessive drinking.
Yet while it is impossible to legislate moderate drinking habits, the feasibility of lowering traffic accidents through enforcement of speed laws has been proven many times.
We need no further invitations to highway recklessness. We need more traffic policemen so that speed limits can be enforced and lives saved.
I might say in this respect, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Highways for the Province of British Columbia has had several convictions for violations of the highway traffic laws. I asked my question to bring to the attention of the House the excellent record established by the City of Trail, in the hope that other cities and communities would be prompted to follow this splendid example, and knowing of the interest of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) in this very important question. maintopic: HIGHWAY SAFETY-TRAIL, B.C., RECORD PERIOD FREE OF FATAL ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), and I judge that the reason the question was directed to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) was because of the fact that his department of the Federal Government is probably more interested in highway safety than the other departments of Government.
May I at this stage express on behalf of the Minister of Public Works and his officials congratulations to the public safety officials of Trail, British Columbia, and to the vehicle travelling public and pedestrians of that city on the splendid record which they have achieved of 3,807 days without a traffic fatality. All departments of the Federal Government co-operate with the Canadian Highway Safety Council, which sponsors an annual Safe Driving Week, and all Federal departments instruct their employees as to the aims and objects of the Safe Driving Week campaign. Their co-operation is solicited for the observance of safe driving habits, not only during the Safe Driving Week but every day throughout the year, toward the reduction in deaths, injuries and loss of property due to highway accidents.
The record of the City of Trail is a tangible example of what can be accomplished in reducing highway traffic accidents by the promotion and observance of safe driving habits. It is hoped that all communities in Canada will in 1965 and in the years to come surpass the splendid record of lOJ years without a traffic fatality, which is enjoyed by the City of Trail, British Columbia.
May I add, Mr. Speaker, one or two other statistics of the Trail record which have not been mentioned. The hon. Member has quoted the number of fatality free days that was established over the last 10J years. I think the record shows that the last fatality occurred on December 5, 1954. That is, as I said, 10J years ago. In 1964 there were only nine injuries, which was the lowest injury rate in Canada for cities between 10,000 and 20,000 population. The City of Trail has qualified for and received a Citation Award every year since the Safety Campaign Awards were first

REDISTRIBUTION-BRITISH COLUMBIA-OPPORTUNITY FOR REPRESENTATIONS TO COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I asked the Minister of Transport what steps the Electoral Boundaries Commissioners for British Columbia had taken to assure that interested persons, such as members of town councils and chambers of commerce, had been made adequately aware of their right to make representations regarding proposed riding changes.
I asked the question, which was directed to be put on the order paper, in no critical sense of the Redistribution Commissioners but really because of a statement made by the Chairman of that Commission-a proper statement to be made by him-in which he is reported to have said that he did not want to make it appear that they had now closed their minds on the subject, because they had not; that the commission would welcome public briefs, and that if the public briefs presented a good case they would make changes.
I asked the question because, in view of the nature of British Columbia, it being far flung and very widespread, I think it is essential, if people are going to be made aware of their rights under the Act to make representations, that the Commission use every possible means to bring these rights of the citizens to their attention.
I hope that the Commission will not use only this means outlined in the Act of publishing its advertisements in the Canada Gazette and one other newspaper. I have seen the advertisements in the Vancouver daily press, very handsome and informative advertisements; but I hope that the Commission will use other means of advertising, for example in the weekly press, possibly direct mailing to mayors, reeves and village chairmen, informing them of their right to be heard by the Redistribution Commissioners at the public hearings to be held.
If this operation of redistribution is to be successful, Mr. Speaker, people must be able to bring before the Commission particular interests in their area. I think it would be
[Mr. McWilliam.J

valuable to put on the record the exact wording of the notice setting out the rights the public has in this matter:
Parliament has provided by virtue of subsection. 4 of section 17 of the said Act, that no representation shall be heard by the Commission at its sitting unless notice in writing has been given, stating the name and address of the person by whom the representation is sought to be made and indicating concisely the nature of the representation and of the interest of such person. Such notice in writing must be given within twenty-three (23) days from the date of publication of this notice, to the Secretary to the Commission, at 615 Ritz Hotel, 1040 West Georgia Street, Vancouver 5, British Columbia.
I think that clearly sets out the rights involved. I hope that the Commission will take every means of advertising this section of the Act so that people in the province of British Columbia who feel they have representations to make to the Commission realize they must submit their names within 23 days from yesterday.
I also asked this question, Mr. Speaker, because of another comment by Mr. Justice Mclnnes, the Chairman of the British Columbia Boundaries Commission, in which he is reported to have said that he hopes it is a good plan and that they spent a lot of time trying to equalize the ridings. I hope that that statement by the learned Judge does not carry the implication it seems to carry-that the Commission simply used a process of mathematics to arrive at the proposed ridings which they have recommended. It seems to me that democracy is far more than a question simply of bloodless mathematics; if the people are to be properly represented as well as communities and their interests, ridings must be workable ridings, must be viable ridings, which Members of Parliament can properly represent in this House. We in this House who passed this legislation recognized this very fact and provided a provincial average or quotient, in the case of British Columbia, of 70,800 per riding which could be varied by the Commissioner by 25 per cent upwards or downwards.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We also provided by section 13(c) two methods by which the Commissioners could vary the average or quotients. I think I should place that provision on the record, Mr. Speaker. It reads as follows:
(c) the commission may depart from the strict application of rules (a) and (b) in any case where
(i) special geographic considerations, including in particular the sparcity, density or relative rate of growth of population of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions or the

size or shape thereof, appear to the commission to render such a departure necessary or desirable, or
(ii) any special community or diversity of interest of the inhabitants of various regions of the province appears to the commission to render such a departure necessary or desirable,-
I have put that on the record because I think some individuals in British Columbia will desire to place representations before the Commission as a result of those two provisos. I am sure many people in the City of Vancouver resident in the riding I represent will wonder about the situation when Vancouver loses one riding, as has been proposed, with the result that the people who live in the riding of Vancouver-Bur-rard will find themselves in the general riding of Vancouver Centre, which will then be the largest riding in British Columbia. They will wonder whether the Commission has taken these provisos into account, particularly in respect of the relative rate of growth of that area of Vancouver in the west end and in Kitsilano. That is the fastest growing area of Vancouver, and every time I go home I see a new high rise apartment breaking the horizon.
